study.title: Exodus 24 The sealed covenant, the manifested presence, and the ascent of Moses
study.overview: Exodus 24 shows the solemn confirmation of the covenant between the LORD and Israel. First, the people hear the terms, respond with agreement and the commitment is recorded in writing. Then the covenant is ratified with sacrifices and blood, pointing to the seriousness of the relationship between holy God and a people called to obey. Then a representative group rises to a certain extent from the mount and receives a vision of the glory of God, but without unrestricted access. Finally, Moses is called to enter the cloud and remains forty days and forty nights on the mount, preparing to receive additional instructions.

outline.title: Call to the mount and acceptance of the covenant
outline.explanation: The LORD determines limits of approach: Moses comes closer, while Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders prostrate in the distance. Moses conveys to the people all the words and statutes; the people answer unanimously that they will obey, publicly assuming the covenant.

outline.title: Record, sacrifice and blood of the covenant
outline.explanation: Moses writes the words of the LORD, raises an altar and pillars representing the tribes, offers sacrifices, and reads the book of the covenant. The blood is sprinkled on the altar and on the people, sealing the covenant. Then Moses and the leaders go up, they see a manifestation of the glory of God and participate in a meal of communion, but without divine holiness being violated.

outline.title: The cloud, the glory and the permanence of Moses in the mount
outline.explanation: God calls Moses to go up and receive tablets of stone with law and commandments written by God. Moses leaves the elders with practical instructions, rises with Joshua as far as the cloud covers the mountain, and the glory of the LORD rests on Sinai. After six days, God calls Moses from the middle of the cloud, and he enters deeper into the divine presence, remaining forty days and forty nights.

study.context: The chapter resumes the Sinai scene after the surrender of the previous words and statutes. The focus here is not only to receive commandments, but to formally confirm the covenant relationship between the Lord and Israel. The notes highlight the mediating function of Moses and the representative participation of the elders and leaders, without allowing the entire people to approach the mountain.
study.theology: The text emphasizes the holiness of God and the need for mediation. The covenant is not treated as something informal: it is proclaimed, written, read and sealed with blood. The people's response shows verbal commitment, but the chapter already suggests that the required obedience is total and that closeness to God depends on his initiative and his holy limits. The partial vision of divine glory indicates that God reveals himself of truth, but not exhaustively; his majesty is accessible only in the terms which he establishes. The meal of the leaders in the presence of God points to communion, but communion marked by reverence. Moses" permanence in the cloud anticipates that the revelation of God will come through his chosen servant, who receives instruction to teach the people. In evangelical Christian reading, the sprinkling of the blood and the mediation of Moses recall that access to God requires atonement and mediation, without reducing the text to a simple social ceremony.

scholarViews.insight: The sprinkling of blood symbolizes God's formal oath to keep the covenant.
Moses acts as a mediator between God and Israel in bringing to the people the words received and sealing the covenant.
Moses ascends with Joshua to the region covered by the cloud and then advances further, while the others remain below.

questions: How does the verbal response of the people in 24:3 and 24:7 relate to the need for concrete obedience throughout the rest of the book?
Why is the covenant ratified with blood, and what does this teach about the seriousness of the relationship with the holy God?
What does the progressive rise of Moses to the mount teach about access, mediation, and reverence before the presence of God?
study.practice: This chapter invites you to treat worship with reverence and obedience with seriousness. The believer can examine whether his confession of faith is only verbal or accompanied by real commitment to the Word of God. He also calls to value God's mediation in revelation: listening, reading, keeping and practicing. In practice, it is an invitation to approach God with fear, gratitude and trust, without trivializing his holiness.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not clarify details of the meaning of sacrifices beyond their function in the ratification of the alliance, nor do they explain in an exhaustive way what exactly the leaders saw in 24:10-11; therefore, the description remains limited to what the text and the comments allow to affirm. It is also not possible to safely determine, from only these notes, all the contours of Joshua's paper during the forty days.
